title: Latent Activation Editing: Inference-Time Refinement of Learned Policies for Safer Multirobot Navigation
models: decentralized IPPO multi-quadrotor navigation policy of Huang et al. (MLP encoders + attention, latent d = 30)
action_head: regression head (four normalized rotor thrusts); not a foundation model
methods: MLP behavior classifier on intermediate latents (unsafe = within H steps of a collision)
latent collision world model (GRU) that predicts future pre-collision latents and substitutes them
baselines: KD-tree retrieval, SAE unit steering, UMAP / Barlow Twins / autoencoder projections, transformer LCWM
ablations over which latent block is edited, horizon H and prediction horizon m
question: Can replacing a frozen RL navigation policy's latents, when flagged as unsafe, with predicted 'more dangerous-looking' future latents make the policy avoid collisions earlier without retraining?
key_findings: On 2,600 configurations where the base policy collides at least once (deterministic sim): collisions 5,623 -> 583 (-89.6%), zero-collision trajectories 0 -> 2,175 (82.7%), robot success 0.58 -> 0.64; paired t-test mean reduction 1.94 per run (95% CI [1.86, 2.01]), p < 1e-300, Cohen's d = 1.0.
Same direction in the stochastic simulator over 10 runs with 95% CIs (Fig. 4).
Alternatives are weaker: KD-tree retrieval 2,678 collisions, SAE unit steering 2,896 (hyperparameter-fragile), UMAP 3,766, Barlow Twins 3,355, plain autoencoder 37,749, transformer LCWM 612.
Editing must spare self-dynamics features: editing only neighbor/obstacle parts of Z1 gives 583 collisions, editing all of Z1 gives 67,951 collisions; editing the downstream Z2 is worse still.
Timing matters: H = 50 -> 1,124 collisions, H = 250 -> 583; prediction horizon m = 10 best, m = 30 -> 60,547 collisions.
Behavior classifier accuracy about 98% (99.3% on safe trajectories); runs onboard Crazyflie 2.1 (<10k params, <1 ms); real-world crossing demos shown qualitatively.

benchmarks: Crazyflie 2.1 bilateral and four-way crossing demos
evidence.scale: 2,600 failure configurations replayed with and without editing; 10 stochastic runs for the non-deterministic check
evidence.statistics: yes for the main comparison: paired t-test, 95% CI, Cohen's d; ablations without tests
evidence.baselines: unedited policy, KD-tree retrieval, SAE steering, encoder-decoder projections, transformer LCWM

causal_validation: Yes, the edit is an intervention on latents and changes closed-loop collisions; the self-vs-environment ablation shows which latent components can be edited safely. The 'amplified risk perception' story is a hypothesis; there is no test that the substituted latents encode risk as such.
closed_loop: Yes, closed-loop multi-agent simulation and onboard hardware.
limitations_stated: Only demonstrated for collision avoidance in multi-quadrotor navigation; other behaviors and platforms left to future work.
Editing horizon H and prediction horizon m are task-dependent hyperparameters.
critique: Evaluation is restricted to configurations where the base policy fails; it is not stated whether these are disjoint from the classifier/LCWM training rollouts, so overfitting to known failure scenes cannot be ruled out.
Small RL controller, not a foundation model; relevant as a precursor showing that monitor-then-edit works and that editing proprioceptive features breaks control.
The finding that SAE-based unit steering was fragile and that safety-relevant information is entangled is a useful negative datapoint for SAE steering claims in VLAs.
Hardware evidence is anecdotal (a few demo runs, no counts).
code: https://lae-robotics.github.io/ (project page says videos and code)
one_line: A small classifier flags unsafe latents in a frozen quadrotor-swarm policy and a GRU swaps in predicted pre-collision latents, cutting simulated collisions by about 90% and running onboard Crazyflies.
